transcript.text: My indesit washing machine fills with water and drains but the drum just doesn't go round at all. Its an IWC something. Had it about 9 years. Is it worth fixing?

Yes—at 9 years old it can still be worth fixing, depending on the fault. On an Indesit IWC, the common causes when it fills and pumps out but the drum never turns are:

1. Drive belt has come off or snapped
   Very common and usually cheap: roughly £10–£25 for the part. A repairer may charge around £80–£140 total.

2. Worn motor carbon brushes
   Also common at this age, especially if the machine has gradually become reluctant to spin. Parts are often £15–£40; fitted repair commonly around £100–£170.

3. Motor, wiring, or control-board fault
   Potentially £150–£250+ depending on parts and labour. At that point, replacement may make more sense for a basic 9-year-old machine.

4. Drum/bearing problem
   Less likely if it simply stopped turning, but if the drum feels rough, loose, noisy, or difficult to turn by hand, it can be uneconomic to repair.

### Quick safe checks
• Unplug it first.
• Open the door and turn the drum by hand. It should rotate fairly smoothly, with only normal resistance.
• Turns freely/easily, but never moves on a cycle: belt, brushes, motor or electronics are likely.
• Stiff, grinding, or wobbly: possible bearing/drum issue.
• If you are comfortable removing the rear panel with the machine unplugged, look for a loose, broken, or missing belt around the large drum pulley and motor pulley. That is the best-case fault.
• Notice whether it makes a humming/clicking sound when it should turn. A hum can point towards motor brushes or a jammed motor; complete silence can suggest wiring/control-board issues.

### Is it worth it?
• Belt or brushes: definitely usually worth repairing.
• Repair quote under about £150: usually reasonable if the machine otherwise works well and is not rusty/leaking/noisy.
• £200 or more for motor/PCB/bearings: generally consider replacing it, unless it is a higher-spec model or you strongly prefer repair.

Find the full model number on the sticker just inside the door opening or at the back—something like IWC 6xxx—and give that, plus whether the drum turns freely by hand and whether you hear a motor hum. That would narrow it down substantially.

I've looked at the label inside the door and it says IWC 71252. With the power off the drum turns freely by hand and is quiet, with no scraping. When it should be turning I can hear relays clicking but no motor noise at all. I did notice a faint hot electrical smell a few weeks ago, but not since.

That narrows it down quite a bit.

For an Indesit IWC 71252, a freely turning, quiet drum makes failed bearings or a seized drum very unlikely. Relays clicking means the control is at least attempting to start the motor. The earlier hot electrical smell is the important clue.

Most likely possibilities, roughly in order:

1. Motor carbon brushes worn out / damaged
• Very plausible at around 9 years old.
• The machine can fill, drain, and click as normal, but the motor does not run.
• Worn brushes can sometimes produce a hot/burning electrical smell before finally failing.
• Usually a worthwhile repair.

2. Burnt or loose motor wiring/connector
• Particularly at the motor plug, wiring loom, or on the control board.
• A poor connection can heat up and smell, then eventually stop supplying the motor.

3. Control-board motor drive fault
• The relays may click but the board may not be sending power properly to the motor, often due to a failed triac, relay contact, resistor, or burnt solder joint.
• This is more likely if there is genuinely no motor hum, twitch, or attempt to move.
• Still repairable, but costs vary.

4. Drive belt off/broken
• Still check this first because it is simple and cheap. However, with a belt fault you would often still hear the motor spinning, so total motor silence makes it slightly less likely.

### What I would do next
1. Stop using it and unplug it, especially given the electrical smell. Do not keep trying cycles in case there is a damaged connection or board component.

2. With it unplugged, remove the rear panel and check:
• Is the belt present, properly seated on the big drum pulley and small motor pulley, and intact?
• Any black dust, melted plastic, browned wiring, or signs of arcing around the motor and its connector?
• Is the motor connector firmly fitted?
• Check the mains plug and socket too for heat marks or burning.

3. If the belt is fine and there are no obvious damaged wires, the next sensible diagnosis is motor brushes and the control board/motor connections. Brushes are fairly accessible for an appliance engineer and may be practical DIY work only if you are confident working around appliance components—always with it unplugged.

### Is it worth fixing?
Yes, I would get a repair quote before replacing it.

• Belt / wiring / brushes: often approximately £90–£160 fitted and worth doing.
• Refurbished/repaired control module: perhaps £140–£220 fitted, potentially still worthwhile if the machine is otherwise sound.
• New control board plus labour or a failed motor: can reach £200–£300+; then replacement becomes more attractive.

When booking someone, describe it specifically as: “Indesit IWC 71252 fills and drains, drum turns freely by hand, relays click but motor is completely silent, and there was a faint electrical burning smell previously.” That should steer them towards checking the motor brushes, motor loom/connector and motor drive circuit rather than looking at pumps or bearings.

I've taken the back panel off with it unplugged. The belt is on both pulleys and feels tight, and the plugs at the motor look pushed in. I can't see anything obviously melted or browned, but I wouldn't know what counts as normal dust. I don't own a multimeter, so I can't test anything electrically. What would you check next?

With the belt intact and the drum free, the next most useful check is the motor carbon brushes. On this type/age of Indesit, they are a common cause of exactly this symptom, and the earlier hot electrical smell fits.

Do not run it with the back off or attempt any live tests without proper equipment.

### 1. Inspect the motor and brushes
With the machine unplugged:

1. Take photos of the motor wiring and belt routing first.
2. Slip the belt off the small motor pulley—turn the large drum pulley by hand while easing the belt off.
3. The motor is normally held by two mounting bolts/screws underneath the drum. Disconnect its plug(s), remove the bolts, and slide the motor out. It can be awkward/heavy, so support it.
4. On either side of the motor will be a brush holder, usually black plastic, with a wire terminal.

You are looking for:

• Very short brushes: if the carbon part is only a few millimetres long, uneven, chipped, or stuck in its holder, they need replacing.
• Normal brush length: a healthy brush normally protrudes noticeably from its holder—often around 10–15 mm or more, though exact dimensions vary.
• Black carbon dust: a light-to-moderate amount of dry black/grey dust around a brushed motor is normal. It is not, by itself, evidence of burning.
• Commutator condition: this is the copper segmented ring the brushes rub on. It should look reasonably even and coppery/darkened from use. Deep grooves, black burnt patches, loose segments, or a strong burnt smell suggest the motor may need more than brushes.

If the brushes are worn, replacing them is generally a sensible DIY repair if you are comfortable removing/refitting the motor. Buy brushes specifically listed for the IWC 71252, ideally using the machine’s full service/serial number from the rating label, as variants can use different motors/brush holders.

### 2. Closely inspect the wiring loom
While the motor is out, trace the wires from it as far as you can see. Look especially where the loom bends or moves with the tub/suspension:

• wire insulation rubbed through;
• a wire partly pulled out of a connector;
• blackened connector pins;
• hardened, melted, or brittle plastic;
• localised burnt smell.

A connector can look plugged in but still have a burnt or loose contact inside, so check whether the plug sits firmly and whether any individual pin looks darker than the others.

### 3. Check the motor turns
With the belt off, turn the small motor pulley/shaft by hand. It should turn smoothly. Some slight “notchy” magnetic feel is normal. It should not be seized, scraping, or exceptionally stiff.

### What I would not do next
I would not start probing the control board, bypassing anything, or trying to power the motor directly. The board and motor circuitry are mains-voltage, and the prior hot-electrical smell means it is especially not a fault to experiment with live.

### Likely decision point
• Brushes clearly worn: replace them; this is very likely worth doing.
• Brushes look healthy and wiring/connectors look sound: the likely suspects become the motor itself or the control board/motor drive. At that point, a repairer who can test the motor and board is preferable to swapping parts blindly.
• Evidence of heat damage: do not use it again until repaired.

If you can describe or photograph the brushes once the motor is out—particularly how much carbon is left—I can help judge whether they are worn enough to explain it.
I've got the motor brushes out. One is very short and blackened or charred at the tip, and the other is a bit longer. Does that sound like enough to explain it?

Yes — that is very likely enough to explain the fault.

Motor brushes should wear at broadly the same rate and maintain firm contact with the commutator. If one is very short and its tip is blackened/charred, it may no longer be touching properly or may be sticking in its holder. The motor then gets no effective current path, so the controller may click but the motor will not run. It also fits the faint hot electrical smell you noticed earlier.

### Before ordering brushes
Check the copper commutator on the motor armature—the segmented copper ring the brush tips run on:

• Usually acceptable: smooth-ish copper or dark brown surface, even all around, no obvious ridges.
• Concerning: deep grooves, badly burnt/blue-black areas, raised or loose copper segments, or lots of melted-looking material.
• Remove loose carbon dust with a dry soft brush or vacuum. Avoid spraying cleaner into the motor, and do not use oily lubricants.
• Make sure each new brush will slide freely in its holder and its spring moves properly.

A slightly dark commutator is normal. If it is merely dirty or lightly darkened, new brushes are normally a reasonable repair.

### Replace both brushes as a matched pair
Do not replace only the short one. Obtain a pair matched to the exact motor, not just the washing-machine model if possible. The motor’s own label will give a manufacturer/type number (often CESET, Sole, or similar), which is the safest way to identify the correct brush set.

When fitting:
• Ensure each brush is oriented the same way as the originals; the angled carbon face must match the commutator’s direction.
• Refit the motor securely, reconnect all plugs, and refit the belt and rear panel.
• New brushes may take a little time to bed in. The first one or two cycles can produce a slight electrical/carbon smell and some sparking internally, but it should not be strong or persistent.

If the commutator is severely damaged, or the new brushes do not restore motor operation, the next likely issue would be a motor fault or control-board/motor wiring problem. But based on what you have found, brushes are the inexpensive and sensible first repair.
